title: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters
hook: Shiva calls the world an illusion, food and all, so Parvati vanishes, and the kitchens of the world go empty
carry: Durga, Kali, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Parvati as characters

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth of Durga's sister goddesses, Parvati, outlasted Shiva at austerity and turned her back on his mockery, until he dropped the disguise.

On Kailash, an argument. Shiva, the great ascetic, is explaining that the world of things is illusion, maya: bodies, houses, possessions, even food, none of it ultimately real. Parvati listens. Then, in the story people tell, she decides to let him find out what that means. She disappears, and with her goes every grain, every loaf, every pot on every stove. The fields stand empty. Creatures go hungry. Even the gods grow faint. Even Shiva. Today, Parvati again, and an argument made without a single word.
screen: `SHIVA: EVEN FOOD IS ILLUSION.` → `PARVATI DISAPPEARS.` → `EVERY KITCHEN GOES EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Word comes that somewhere food is still being served. In Kashi, the holy city of Varanasi, a kitchen is open, and at its door stands a goddess with a ladle and a pot that never runs out, feeding everyone who comes. Her name in this story is Annapurna, which tradition explains as the one who is full of food. So Shiva, lord of the universe, the great ascetic who said food was unreal, walks to Kashi with a begging bowl and holds it out to her. And she fills it. The images of this moment are tender, not triumphant: the goddess serving, the god receiving, a family meal. Some tellers say Shiva learned that the body and its hunger aren't to be waved away. Some say Parvati wasn't arguing against his teaching at all, but filling it out: in that reading, spirit needs a body to live in, and a body needs to eat. In Varanasi a temple to Annapurna stands near Shiva's own, and devotees speak of her as the mother who makes sure no one in the city goes hungry. And with that the five are met: the warrior, the fierce mother, the one who chooses, the hidden river, and now the cook at the door in Kashi, filling Shiva's bowl. Five characters, and some Hindus would add, one power moving through them all. That's tomorrow's question.
screen: `A KITCHEN STILL OPEN IN KASHI.` · `ANNAPURNA, THE ONE FULL OF FOOD.` · `SHIVA HOLDS OUT A BEGGING BOWL.` · then, large: `SHE FILLS IT.` · then: `FIVE CHARACTERS, MET.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the last thing you ate and trace it back: who cooked it, who carried it, who grew it, the rain, the soil, letting the chain be long. Then notice the body that received it, using it right now to breathe. If you pray, thank Annapurna or God for food in your own words; if you don't, just thank the hands.
Durga. The name over all five goddesses met in this run; today, the Goddess as Annapurna, filling Shiva's bowl. Today's word.

howItsDone: Annapurna is honored in homes and kitchens as the goddess of nourishment, and her temple in Varanasi stands near the Kashi Vishwanath temple of Shiva; some families offer a little food to her before a meal.

original.note: Sanskrit: Annapurna; tradition explains the name as 'she who is full of food,' and knows her as a form of Parvati.

chat.says: Why does Shiva go begging for food from Annapurna?
options: Parvati vanished with all the food after he called it illusion; only her kitchen was open.
His own kitchen on Kailash burned down, and Kashi was the nearest place.
Kashi's kings banned him from their kitchens, so he had to ask a goddess.
chat.meaning: In the story people tell, Parvati vanishes with every grain after Shiva calls food illusion; as Annapurna in Kashi, she fills his bowl.
